title: Recipe Undo
statement: A recipe app records steps a cook adds, and an Undo button that removes the most recently added step still in the recipe. Given the list of actions, return the final steps in order.
examples: add flour, add eggs, undo, add milk gives flour, milk
undo with no steps does nothing

approaches.name: Keep the steps on a stack
approaches.hint: The newest item is the one that leaves
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Add pushes, Undo pops: each action is O(1), and the stack holds exactly the steps that remain, in order.

approaches.name: After each undo, rebuild the recipe from all actions so far
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Correct, but every undo replays the whole history.

approaches.name: Keep the steps in a queue and remove from the front on undo
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Undo would remove the oldest step instead of the newest, which gives the wrong recipe.

title: Print Room
statement: A library printer receives jobs during the day and must print them in the order they arrived. Each job may be sent back to the end of the line if the paper runs out. Choose how to store the waiting jobs so the day's 100,000 jobs run fast.
examples: jobs A, B, C print as A, B, C
a job sent back prints after the jobs already waiting

approaches.name: A queue: an array with a head index, or a deque
approaches.hint: Take from the front without moving the rest
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Adding at the back and taking from the front are both O(1), and the order is first in, first out.

approaches.name: An array with push() and shift()
approaches.hint: Use the built-in methods as they are
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: The order is right, but each shift() moves every waiting job, so a busy day becomes slow.

approaches.name: A stack: push and pop at the end
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: The newest job would print first, which breaks arrival order.

title: Tag Check
statement:
A simple web page editor checks that tags such as , , and

are closed in the right order: inner tags close before outer ones. Given the list of opening and closing tags, decide whether the page is well formed.

approaches.name: A stack of open tags; each closing tag must match the top
approaches.hint: Check against the most recent open item
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: The tag that must close next is always the most recently opened one, which is the top of the stack.

approaches.name: Repeatedly delete a matching open-close pair that sit next to each other
approaches.hint: Shrink the list until nothing changes
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Correct, but each pass scans the list again.

approaches.name: Count opening and closing tags of each kind
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Equal counts do not prove the order: has equal counts but is not well formed.
